doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23

title: Former band members and teaching Chink Martin tuba
summary: Laine names surviving sidemen, tells how he put a borrowed tuba in Chink Martin's hands, and mentions Manuel Alexander and Ernest Stevens.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: He knows it. Do you remember who some of the men were in your band back in those days that did play a funeral?
Do I remember some of them? You remember some of your men. I remember some of them. Back of the day. Yeah, you must remember a lot of them. Sure I do. Yeah. You must.
Most of them are dead. Yeah. There's only two of them living. You like to take Richard Brunish and Marlowe and... Jimmy Kennel just died.
Jimmy Kennel died too about two months ago.
Yeah, he just died. Most of them, the Brunish boys are living.
What about Chinka Martin? He's living. He's living. He's living. Oh yeah. He played with you in the old days.

Oh yeah. Here's a queer thing. This is a really coincidence. Yeah, it seems. I had a man by the name of Kaskrow playing bass with me, you know. And he took very sick. And that takes me one of them Wild West show jobs. And I needed a tuba player. See? So Kaskrow couldn't play. He was sick. Down and out couldn't play. So I borrowed the horn from him. See? Yeah. And I stuck it in Chink's hand. I said, whether you know or not, I said, you're going to learn this thing. Yes or no? For me? You're going to learn it? He said, I don't know nothing about that. I said, you're going to learn it? Take it. He stood up there and he started pumping in it. Of course, the band drowned them. You know, false notes and all that. Drowned them. But don't you know that it was no time at all that Chink Martin could handle that bass as good, that bass horn as good as any man in this man's town? So I went to Kaskrow and I said, Joe, I said, you've all washed up. I said, how about selling me that tuba? He said, yeah, something sell it to you. Give me eight dollars for it. Give me eight dollars for it. Give it to Chink Martin. And brother, he made a tuba player. There ain't no question about it. Then I had this fella Alexander, Joe Alexander playing tuba with me too, you know. He was a pretty good tuba. He used to play a hurricane tuba. See?
Oh, yes. One of those. One of the guys.

Played one of them tubas. Now, his son too, you know. His son Manuel, the fella that's a professor today. He played with me too. He's living. Manuel, ain't he living? Who? Manuel Alexander. Manuel Alexander.
You told me you met him, yeah. I don't know. I've never seen him.
Well, he played with me too. He trained out to be a professor of music.
Yeah, he's teaching in some college. Oh, yeah. Then we're doing, isn't he? Yeah. Manuel.
Now, Ernest Stevens, he's living. He played with me too.
Yeah, Ernest Stevens. He come here.
Is he still here in town? Yeah. He's got his own home back in Gentilly somewheres. I got his address. I got his telephone number. Yes, we'd like to look him up sometime too.
